articles.title: GTA 6, Resident Evil 9, AI and EA: Gaming trends to watch in 2026
articles.summary: Next year could be hugely significant for video games - here are the big things to keep an eye on.
articles.body:
The video games industry is unpredictable.

If you'd told us this time last year that a previously unknown French studio would claim game of the year, Battlefield 6 would knock Call of Duty off the top of the annual charts and that Saudi Arabia would buy gaming giant Electronic Arts (EA) we'd have been... sceptical.

So you'd have to be very sure of yourself - or very foolish - to try and predict what's going to happen in the year ahead.

Luckily, we're not in the crystal ball business here at BBC Newsbeat, but there are a few things we can be confident video game fans should keep an eye on in 2026.

Whether it’s big releases, big moves or big issues - here’s a rundown of some of the most important things to look out for.

"A cultural moment, a day millions of players have been awaiting for a very, very long time."

Sound familiar? It should. It's what we wrote about Grand Theft Auto 6 this time last year .

Two delays and one new trailer later, and we're more or less where we were 12 months ago.

Assuming it comes out, as planned, on 19 November, it will almost certainly break records.

And you can bet other publishers will want to release their own 2026 games as far away from it as possible.

But the big question remains: "Will it get delayed again?"

Publisher Take Two says it's confident the new date will hold, but it remains to be seen whether developer Rockstar's recent sacking of 31 staff - which included experienced team members - will affect the game.

Resident Evil 9, James Bond and Wolverine

Like this year, when publishers manoeuvered around GTA 6's original "late 2025" release date, 2026 is front-loaded with significant releases.

Japanese giant Capcom unleashes Resident Evil Requiem , the ninth main entry in its blockbuster horror series, in February, followed by sci-fi action adventure Pragmata in April.

Sony is also planning to drop PlayStation exclusive Saros , a follow-up to 2021's widely-praised Returnal, in April.

While Wolverine, the next superhero smash from Spider-Man studio Insomniac - another in-house Sony developer - is set to arrive in the autumn.

May will see the arrival of 007 First Light - the celeb-filled James Bond adventure from Hitman developer IO Interactive.

Nintendo will be looking to maintain the momentum of its record-breaking Switch 2 launch this year.

Ones to watch include Pokopia - a cosy take on Pokémon - and online multiplayer The Duskbloods from Elden Ring maker FromSoftware.

Fans have complained about the lack of a brand new Mario or Zelda game and, as things stand, neither has been announced yet. But the company's got form for announcing big new games mere months before they release.

Microsoft recently teased big reveals for its January 2026 Developer Direct showcase and, unless we're told otherwise, is due to release Fable - its reboot of the very British fantasy RPG series - and Gears of War: E-Day sometime during the year.

Marking 25 years of its Xbox brand could also give the company a chance to win back fans after backlashes over studio closures, price rises to its Game Pass subscription service and its decision to release flagship series on rival consoles .

And that's just the major publishers. Expect more indie surprises to take centre stage next year.

Our one-to-watch is Raccoin - a score attack game inspired by arcade coin-pusher machines.

Random-access memory, or RAM, is a vital component in millions of electronic devices including smartphones, Smart TVs, medical equipment and even cars.

It's also been getting really, really expensive.

Demand from Artificial Intelligence (AI) data centre projects has been blamed, with some of the world's biggest RAM manufacturers pivoting towards supplying demand from big tech firms.

Micron, owner of the Crucial brand sold in many online and high street shops, recently announced it was ceasing its consumer business to focus on demand from AI companies.

All of which has created a shortage that, according to some analysts, could eventually push up prices of electronics, with video game consoles high on the list of potential casualties.

Business website Bloomberg reported that production costs for Nintendo's Switch 2 could rise and there are also concerns that Valve's upcoming PC-console hybrid Steam Machine could be delayed, or more expensive, as a result of the situation.

So far, no video game companies have commented.

In the games industry, which has faced thousands of layoffs in recent years, discussions about generative AI (GenAI) and its impact on jobs are especially fierce.

Just this month Swen Vincke, the boss of multi-award-winning Baldur's Gate 3 maker Larian Studios, faced a backlash when he told interviewers the company had explored using GenAI for coming up with ideas and early prototypes.

He said no AI content would appear in its finished games nor replace human workers but, in a follow-up response, said it would be "irresponsible" not to assess new technologies.

Despite early claims that GenAI could allow people to make games more quickly at a fraction of the current costs, it's unclear how much of an impact it's actually had.

Developers who've spoken to BBC Newsbeat say it's not widely used in finished products due to a mix of ethical, legal and practical concerns, but plenty of companies have at least tried using it for pre-production work.

Some smaller companies proudly state that they don't use the tools at any stage of development.

Against a backdrop of uncertainty over the long-term future of GenAI , it remains to be seen how far its use will spread.

But it's a topic that fosters strong emotions from players and workers within the industry, so expect more controversies as the year ploughs on.

Electronic Arts (EA), the publisher of Battlefield 6, EA FC and The Sims, is one of the world's biggest video game companies, responsible for titles that regularly top bestseller charts.

The announcement it had accepted a record-breaking $55bn (£41bn) bid from a Saudi Arabia-led investment group came as a shock.

It's the country's latest big move into gaming, which it says is part of wider efforts to make its economy less reliant on oil.

But critics believe it's a form of "sportswashing" - investing in entertainment in an attempt to soften its international reputation due to its anti-LGBT laws and human rights record.

The country's conservative cultural values have prompted concerns over the impact the deal could have on certain EA series.

The Sims, which has a big LGBT fanbase, faced a revolt from some of its best-known content creators when some cut official ties in protest against the buyout.

EA replied with a statement saying the game would "always be a space where you can express your authentic self".

There are also concerns that the deal could result in further lay-offs at EA, which has taken on $20bn of debt to finance the purchase.

If all goes to plan, the deal should be completed by the summer, when there should be more clarity on the future of some of gaming's most popular series.

articles.title: Google takes control of ‘Android of robotics’ project in quest for physical AI
articles.summary: Intrinsic is focused on making robots easier to program, teach, and operate.
articles.body: Google is folding Alphabet’s AI robotics “moonshot,” Intrinsic, into the company after five years as an independent unit. The move marks a strategic shift as Google doubles down on physical AI and pulls experimental projects closer to its core business. Intrinsic “graduated” into an independent company inside Alphabet’s Other Bets division in 2021, a portfolio of high-risk, speculative ventures that also includes robotaxi firm Waymo and healthcare company Verily. It pitches itself as an Android-like layer for robotics, building software and tools that make it easier to create robot applications. Details of the purchase are not clear but the companies said Intrinsic will remain a “distinct group within Google.” It will work closely with Google DeepMind and utilize Google’s Gemini AI models and cloud resources, they said. DeepMind absorbed Alphabet’s shuttered Everyday Robotics division in 2023 and last year launched two AI models to help robots perform physical tasks.

articles.title: Google DeepMind’s new AI model can control a robot’s entire body
articles.summary: Google DeepMind has announced its new Gemini Robotics 2 model, which can control a humanoid robot’s entire body.
articles.body: Google DeepMind says the latest version of its Gemini Robotics AI model can “control entire humanoid robots.” While the previous model focused on controlling a humanoid robot’s upper body, Gemini Robotics 2 now supports “whole-body motions” ranging from its feet to fingertips, according to an announcement on Thursday. The new model will allow humanoid robots to perform a wider range of actions, as it allows them to walk, crouch, stretch, and manipulate objects. Videos shared by Google show how Apptronik’s Apollo 2 robot can bend over to pick up a watering can, as well as find and take specific items off a shelf. [Media: Though Google DeepMind notes that its robots “have more to advance in movement speed,” it adds that this update “is an important step towards the skills needed to complete more complex, real-world tasks that require whole-body coordination.” Additionally, Gemini Robotics 2 supports better dexterity, as it can now control more complex, five-fingered hands. That enables robots to perform tasks like sealing a Ziploc, tying a trash bag, or unscrewing a lightbulb. [Media: Google DeepMind is updating Gemini Robotics ER (embodied reasoning) as well, a vision-language model that helps robots to analyze their surroundings, process instructions, and perform multi-step tasks. Gemini Robotics ER 2 is better at completing tasks over an extended period of time and “now understands when tasks begin and end.” Google DeepMind says this update also allows multiple robots of different types to work together and complete tasks, with one video showing how Apollo 2 instructs Google’s dual-arm robot to put tools inside a bin while cleaning the garage. [Media: The company notes Gemini Robotics ER 2 is its “safest robotics model to date,” as it can “better detect when humans are nearby, trigger safety tool calls and bring the robot to a safe stop if someone approaches too closely.” Meanwhile, Google DeepMind has brought improvements to its Gemini Robotics On-Device Model, which can run locally on a robot without an internet connection. This model can now adapt to new embodiments faster, including those with “drastically different shapes, sensors and degrees of freedom.”

articles.title: AI agent reportedly wipes entire season of Swedish TV show before premiere — as presenter says 'I knew AI would be the death of me'
articles.summary: An AI agent reportedly deleted an entire season of a Swedish TV show just weeks before its premiere.
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

The Challenge Sverige has been delayed just weeks before launching

The producers blame a "technical breakdown" that deleted an entire season

Reports suggest an AI agent might have been responsible for the incident

Another day, another report of a faulty AI agent apparently deleting a lot of work. Except this time, instead of nuking 48,000 files from a personal project as we've seen before, the victim is one of Sweden's biggest TV shows.

According to the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet , Mastiff, the production company behind The Challenge Sverige , were putting the final touches on the show — which was due to premiere on November 22 — when it decided to "let an AI agent into the server." After that, the worst-case scenario ensued: the AI agent apparently deleted the entire edited show, with no chance to recover the files.

At least, that's according to Aftonbladet's sources. TV4, the channel set to host The Challenge Sverige , has merely confirmed that there was a "technical breakdown" that resulted in the show's files being deleted. It has not admitted that an AI agent caused the catastrophic incident.

We've asked both TV4 and Mastiff for an official comment on what happened and will update this story when we hear back. But whatever caused the issues, the mishap means that the show has been pushed back from its imminent release to some time in 2027, with no solid date yet announced.

As a result, "Several hundred days of work is now gone and several hundred people now need to go in and work on this to be able to deliver the program," Aftonbladet explained.

Lots of questions remain about this apparent televisual disaster. Was an AI agent definitely the culprit? If so, what exactly was the AI told to do? And what happened to the backup files of a nationally broadcast show that has taken a huge amount of time and effort to create? Some of these details will hopefully be filled in by a response from TV4 and Mastiff, which we've requested.

When Aftonbladet called The Challenge Sverige 's presenter, Ahmed Berhan, Berhan seemed amused by the development. "You know, some days you just have to accept that you're living in a f*cking sitcom," the presenter laughed when he recounted how he was told that the show's files had been obliterated. When Aftonbladet suggested that an AI agent might have been responsible, an incredulous Berhan replied: "Is that true?! I knew AI would be the death of me. This is just the beginning."

If AI agents were indeed involved, the whole sorry saga is a reminder of the risks of letting them loose on vital files that you can't afford to lose. Just a few weeks ago we saw how Claude Code deleted nearly 50,000 files in just 103 seconds when a developer set it to work, and you don't have to look far to see stories of AI agents hacking governments and leaking private data .

articles.title: OpenAI acusa ex-funcionário de vazar segredos para a Apple | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a criadora do ChatGPT, ele enviou mais de 100 arquivos para uma conta pessoal e apresentou o projeto à direção da Apple. Fabricante do iPhone nega ter encontrado evidências.
articles.summary: OpenAI acusa ex-funcionário de transferir arquivos de um aparelho inédito para a Apple, que nega posse de dados confidenciais ou segredos comerciais da concorrente.
articles.body:
O logotipo da OpenAI é visto em um telefone celular em frente a uma tela de computador que exibe a tela inicial do ChatGPT — Foto: AP/Michael Dwyer, Arquivo

A OpenAI acusa um ex-funcionário de ter transferido para uma conta pessoal mais de 100 arquivos da empresa sobre um aparelho ainda não lançado. Ele deixou a criadora do ChatGPT para trabalhar na Apple .

Segundo a OpenAI , o ex-colaborador fez uma apresentação sobre o produto para a alta direção da dona do iPhone.

A acusação consta de um documento apresentado pela OpenAI a um tribunal federal em San Jose, na Califórnia, nos Estados Unidos.

A empresa afirma que a apresentação ocorreu meses atrás e que a Apple agora desenvolve seus próprios produtos de inteligência artificial. Como exemplo, cita o lançamento do HomeView nesta semana .

"A OpenAI está muito preocupada com o fato de seus segredos comerciais e informações confidenciais estarem circulando dentro da Apple , onde os engenheiros deles podem moldar os próximos produtos da empresa com base no trabalho confidencial e inovador da OpenAI ", afirmou a criadora do ChatGPT no documento.

A Apple disse que tem políticas e procedimentos para garantir que novos funcionários não utilizem informações confidenciais de empregadores anteriores. A empresa afirmou ainda que não encontrou evidências que sustentem as acusações da OpenAI .

articles.title: Anthropic is making Claude ‘election-ready’ as US mid-term polls near; company says: Goal is to prevent …
articles.summary: Anthropic is preparing Claude for the US midterm elections.
articles.body: Anthropic is preparing Claude for the US midterm elections. The artificial intelligence (AI) company said it is bringing new safeguards to prevent election-related misinformation, political manipulation and attempts to interfere with voting. The measures include integrating official voting information into chatbot responses, providing updated election results, and improving systems to detect coordinated AI campaigns that try to influence voters.​Anthropic is also expanding its political-bias measures to ensure Claude responds more evenly across political viewpoints. The company said it plans to make Claude useful in political conversations while also preventing abuse that could harm the democratic process. It follows investigations that revealed attempts to use Claude to produce misleading election coverage and fake news content.​Claude to provide official voting information​Anthropic analysed about 250,000 conversations over one week to understand how people use Claude for political queries. According to the company, discussions about politics, public policy and social issues accounted for 5.75% of conversations on Claude.ai in the US, while election and voting queries represented 0.51%.​Requests asking Claude whom or what to vote for accounted for around 0.01% of conversations, while requests violating its election integrity policies appeared in approximately 0.002%.​Claude.ai will continue directing users to TurboVote, a nonpartisan voting information resource operated by Democracy Works. The chatbot will also begin providing official, state-specific information about polling locations, registration and identification requirements. Anthropic plans to share updated election results and vote counts directly in conversations on election night and in the days that follow.​Anthropic expands political bias testing​Anthropic said Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 scored 99% on its political evenhandedness evaluation.​The company also worked with independent organisations, including Vanderbilt University's Future of Free Speech, the Foundation for American Innovation, and the Collective Intelligence Project, to assess how Claude handles contentious political topics.​The evaluations found that Claude generally engaged with political questions but sometimes added unsolicited caveats or opposing arguments. Another assessment found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 was more likely to soften arguments supporting right-leaning positions.​Anthropic said it has improved how the chatbot presents counterarguments and responds better to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers.​New safeguards target election manipulation​Anthropic's Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to spread false voting information, impersonate election officials or suppress voter participation. It also restricts fake social media profiles, mass-generated comments designed to inflate engagement and content falsely presented as independent journalism.​Working with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and the McCain Institute, Anthropic tested its safeguards against election-related misuse in the US, Israel and Brazil. Researchers found that Claude generally refused direct harmful requests but could miss coordinated campaigns when individual tasks appeared harmless.​The company has since introduced additional detection systems targeting fake accounts, misleading news websites, foreign state-linked operations and cyber threats involving election infrastructure.​Anthropic identifies election-related abuse​Anthropic said foreign-based operators used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favouring Russian, Iranian and North Korean narratives through a fake news website. It also identified attempts to generate fabricated news to attract American audiences and earn advertising revenue.​The company said it banned the accounts involved and improved its detection systems. Anthropic plans to continue strengthening election safeguards and publish further analysis of how people use Claude during the election cycle.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: TSMC Q3 profit surges to record high on AI demand; says considering Texas fab
articles.summary: Investing.com-- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, clocked a stronger-than-expected third-quarter profit on Thursday, with earnings hitting anot...
articles.body:
Investing.com-- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, clocked a stronger-than-expected third-quarter profit on Thursday, with earnings hitting another record high on robust demand from the artificial intelligence industry.

The company said that it had considered setting up more facilities in the U.S., potentially in Texas, as it races to ramp up capacity and meet increasing demand.

The world's largest contract chipmaker said net profit surged to T$763.06 billion ($23.55 billion) in the three months to September 30. The print jumped nearly 69% year-on-year to a record high, and was also well above Reuters/LSEG estimates of T$746.3 billion.

Revenue jumped 50% to T$1.49 trillion. Gross margin was 66.4%, operating margin was 58.7%, and net profit margin was 51.1%, TSMC said.

Capacity buildout to dent margins, TSMC looking at Texas fab

Speaking in a post-earnings webcast, CFO Wendell Huang warned of a continued deterioration in TSMC's gross margins from the company's attempts to increase capacity-- both at home and abroad-- to meet growing chip demand.

Gross margin dilution from the buildout is expected to be closer to 2% in 2026, Huang said, while margin dilution from its overseas facilities was expected to be higher in the coming years. He forecast an at least 0.4% drop in fourth-quarter gross margin.

He said that capital spending was expected to be "significantly higher" in the coming years, citing continued, outsized demand from AI, which required more production capacity.

Huang reiterated TSMC's 2026 capital budget of between $60 billion and $65 billion. He declined to provide a number on just how much capacity will increase in the coming months.

"We're working very hard to increase our capacity in the U.S.," CEO C.C. Wei said in response to an analyst question. Wei said the company had looked at U.S.-based locations outside its primary Arizona site in the U.S., including in Texas, for more facilities.

Wei said the company was still in discussions over the nature of the facilities, on whether they will be run directly by TSMC or as part of a tie-up with partners such as Elon Musk's Terrafab.

Huang said TSMC revenue will be between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 58% year-on-year increase.

articles.title: FBI gives update on spy device found at OpenAI's office; says: Saudi National arrested; shares 'crime photos'
articles.summary: OpenAI fired an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices.
articles.body: OpenAI fired an employee after a hidden recording device was discovered inside one of its San Francisco offices. Now, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has shared an official press release sharing an update on the spy device found at the ChatGPT-maker’s office. It stated that the agency had arrested Abdulrahman Alfozan, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia on October 9. The 35-year-old has been charged with using an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept communications. As stated in the release, FBI Director Kash Patel said that “Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” saidOpenAI employees concealed spy device in toilet paperAs per the release, Abdulrahman Alfozan was employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about September 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. The device was concealed in toilet paper and was installed on or about September 28, the company determined. The recording were encrypted, the agency said.Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where the device was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.According to the complaint, prior to September 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse submitted prompts between September 24 and September 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things.The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between September 27 and September 28, the agency added.OpenAI also alleges that Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building on October 5. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered Alfozan’s wallet, ID and another recording device among other things.If convicted, Alfozan can face a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.You use AI every day. articles.title: AI Race Puts $3.5 Trillion at Write-Down Risk, Gartner Warns
articles.summary: More than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as the industry’s investment boom threatens to outpace the reven...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- More than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as the industry's investment boom threatens to outpace the revenue required to justify it, according to an analysis by market research firm Gartner Inc.

AI data center owners would need to generate a cumulative $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030 to cover capital spending, financing costs and achieve a 12% return on invested capital. Yet Gartner forecasts no more than $3.6 trillion in attributable enterprise and consumer AI revenue over that period — less than half the required amount.

The widening gulf between investment requirements and projected revenue raises questions over the sustainability of the AI infrastructure boom, particularly as rapidly depreciating computing assets risk becoming obsolete before generating sufficient returns.

The implications are especially stark for specialist AI infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV. Their business models are more directly exposed to demand for computing capacity than diversified hyperscalers like Microsoft Corp, Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc.

Gartner predicts that cost pressures and limited differentiation will force more than 80% of neocloud providers to cease operating independently by 2030.

Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said many of these neocloud providers are working to develop the higher-margin software and services of cloud providers, though few may succeed.

"All of them want to be the full-stack. They can't all be," he said. "For every dollar that's spent on compute, only a fraction of that is going to the owners of compute."
authors: Ruhell Amin, Neil Campling and Mark Bergen

articles.title: Ralph Lauren ties executive payouts to AI in sign of retail's shifting priorities
articles.summary: By Danielle Kaye NEW YORK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Ralph Lauren, like many companies in the retail space, had until last year tied part of its executives’ compens...
articles.body:
NEW YORK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Ralph Lauren, like many companies in the retail space, had until last year tied part of its executives' compensation to a warm-and-cuddly metric known as "citizenship and sustainability."

But in a sign of the times, the fashion label has replaced the sustainability measure with one ‌linking a portion of its top leaders' annual payout to "AI metrics."

The company's previously unreported move eliminates sustainability targets — a hallmark of the so-called ESG movement, which urged companies ‌to find performance measures tied to environmental and social well-being — from its short-term incentive plan. Those targets had been in place for four years.

Instead, AI goals were added to a series of other factors, such as sales ​growth and operational costs, as a basis to adjust annual incentive payouts for executives. Buried in a 131-page disclosure, the shift signals an emerging push in the retail sector to hold corporate leaders accountable for AI adoption.

A Ralph Lauren spokesperson said the AI target reinforced "opportunities for leveraging AI to enhance our work."

The company's prior sustainability metrics, she added, contributed to meaningful progress on its goals. "Our work in this area has matured and is now operationalized throughout our business," she said.

Ralph Lauren is among the few publicly listed retailers that have explicitly incorporated AI into incentive plans, joining companies ‌beyond the retail sector including Salesforce and Textron, which also ⁠replaced its ESG metric. A handful of consumer companies, including PepsiCo, have cited advancing an "AI agenda" this year as a factor in setting annual payouts for specific executives.

Compensation advisors say more of Ralph Lauren's peers might eventually follow suit as investors seek returns on AI spending and as consumer companies ⁠turn to the technology to boost margins.

"I'd call it an emerging practice," said Cory Morrow, a partner at Korn Ferry who leads the firm's consumer and retail practice for executive pay.

"The hard part, when you're putting something like AI in a bonus plan, is quantifying what are you really measuring," he said. "It's still relatively new at this point, so companies are just getting a baseline on anything that's ​measurable."

A ​retailer's annual incentive plan is a "messaging device" to signal what's important to the company, Morrow said, adding ​that financial metrics like sales growth and profitability will continue to ‌form the bulk of most bonus plans.

articles.title: Why not knowing may be your greatest strength: Santhosh Jayaram’s book challenges conventional ideas of intelligence and leadership
articles.summary: What if admitting “I don't know” is not a sign of weakness but the beginning of meaningful learning?
articles.body: What if admitting “I don't know” is not a sign of weakness but the beginning of meaningful learning? In a world where artificial intelligence can produce answers in seconds and professional knowledge can quickly become outdated, Santhosh Jayaram’s 'Operating from the Zone of Incompetence: Why Not-Knowing Is the New Intelligence' arrives with a timely question: how do we keep learning when what we already know is no longer enough?Published by Rupa Publications in 2026, the non-fiction book challenges the assumption that expertise alone is the key to progress. Rather than dismissing competence, Jayaram asks readers to consider what happens when they become too comfortable with their existing knowledge. The book’s central idea is that intellectual humility, curiosity and a willingness to unlearn may be essential abilities in a rapidly changing world. Drawing on the themes outlined in his announcement of the book, Jayaram positions learning as a continuous process rather than a destination. The premise is particularly relevant to professionals, leaders and anyone navigating a workplace increasingly shaped by technology and artificial intelligence.Why the comfort of expertise can become a limitationBeing good at something often brings confidence, recognition and a sense of security. But that confidence can also make it harder to question familiar methods or recognise when circumstances have changed. Jayaram’s title captures this tension. Operating from a “zone of incompetence” does not mean abandoning skills or celebrating ignorance. Instead, it suggests being willing to enter unfamiliar territory, ask questions and accept that there is more to learn.This idea challenges a common professional instinct: the pressure to appear knowledgeable at all times. In workplaces where leaders are expected to have answers and employees may fear looking inexperienced, admitting uncertainty can feel risky. Yet refusing to acknowledge knowledge gaps can make people less receptive to new ideas. The book explores what happens when expertise expires, why unlearning can be difficult and how people can continue learning even after achieving professional success. These questions give its central argument practical relevance, especially for people whose careers depend on adapting to changing technologies, expectations and ways of working.Unlearning, leadership and the age of AIOne of the book’s key themes is the importance of unlearning. Acquiring new information is only part of learning; people must sometimes question assumptions, habits and beliefs that once helped them succeed but may no longer be useful. Jayaram traces the beginning of the book to advice from Professor Deepak Gupta, who told him during the early stages of his PhD journey: “You can't learn anything new until you de-learn.” Jayaram said the conversation planted the seed for the book. The title came from a phrase used by Dr R Balasubramaniam during a talk. Jayaram asked to use it, and Balasubramaniam agreed. Both later contributed forewords to the book.The focus on unlearning also connects to the book’s questions about leadership. A leader who believes they must always be right may struggle to invite disagreement or acknowledge changing realities. By contrast, a leader who can say “I don't know. Yet” creates room for inquiry, collaboration and better-informed decisions. This is especially pertinent in the age of AI. As technology makes information easier to access and generate, the ability to ask useful questions, evaluate answers and recognise limitations becomes increasingly important. Access to information does not automatically translate into sound judgement.A reminder to remain an infinite learnerJayaram describes the book as an exploration of intellectual humility, curiosity, adaptability and becoming an “infinite learner”. Rather than telling readers what they should know, he says he wants to change how they relate to what they do not know. That distinction is the book’s most compelling promise. It shifts the focus from collecting qualifications or accumulating expertise to developing an attitude that remains open to revision. For students, this could mean treating mistakes as opportunities to improve. For professionals, it could mean questioning familiar routines. For leaders, it could mean making space for people who challenge established thinking.The idea is not entirely new: lifelong learning and intellectual humility have long been discussed in education and leadership. The strength of Jayaram’s framing lies in placing these ideas against a contemporary backdrop of rapid technological change and the growing uncertainty around which skills will remain relevant. A critical assessment of how successfully the book develops its arguments, supports them with examples and translates them into practical guidance would require examining the full text. Based on its stated themes, however, it offers a useful starting point for readers willing to question the pressure to appear competent all the time.Operating from the Zone of Incompetence ultimately invites readers to see uncertainty not as a dead end, but as an opening. Its message is simple: intelligence is not only about what we know, but also about how honestly we recognise what we have yet to learn.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Google launches its ‘universal’ online shopping cart ahead of the holidays
articles.summary: Google’s intelligent AI shopping cart is finally here, and just in time to tempt users amid Black Friday and seasonal holiday spending.
articles.body: Google’s intelligent AI shopping cart is finally here, and just in time to tempt users into Black Friday and seasonal holiday spending. The Universal Cart tool Google previewed at its I/O event in May is now rolling out in the US across the Gemini app and Google Search, with the aim of making it easier to stay organized and save money when shopping online. As the name suggests, it’s a “universal” digital cart that lets you save products from multiple retailers in a single unified space, and works across different Google platforms. That means you can find and add a bunch of products using the Gemini app and Google Search AI Mode, and they’ll all be saved to the same cart. There are also plans to integrate Universal Cart with Gmail and YouTube, but Google hasn’t announced a timeline for that yet. [Image: Here’s a demo of the checkout options for Universal Cart, which suggest you can’t check out multiple retailers simultaneously. Google will send you notifications about price drops and restocks for items saved in your cart, which spares you from having to check each retailer’s website individually, and can display any relevant promotional codes it finds besides the products you’ve saved. You can choose to pay for items from the cart using Google Wallet, or transfer them to the merchant’s own cart so you can checkout with the retailer directly. Together with Google Wallet, Universal Cart can also analyze the perks provided by each of your saved credit cards and help you choose the best payment method when purchasing. The launch comes as competition in the AI-assisted shopping space is heating up, with Google rivals including OpenAI and Meta having launched agentic AI assistants that can shop online on the user’s behalf. Shopify also recently announced that it’s opening its platform up to allow more AI agents to browse and purchase from Shopify listings. Big Tech players are entering this race on the bet that the future of online shopping involves having a robot do most of the work for you.

articles.title: Nobody is safe from celebrity AI deepfakes
articles.summary: On Instagram and other social media platforms, AI-generated imagery of celebrities is everywhere. A recent fake post depicting actress Mia Goth shows how it can spiral into confusion.
articles.body: In hindsight, the post on Instagram should have raised more red flags. The image purported to show actress Mia Goth, just days after filing for divorce from actor and filmmaker Shia LaBeouf, posing in a T-shirt with a pointed message: MY EX IS MY BIGGEST FAN. To really drive home the point, the song “Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It)” by Beyoncé was added to the post. It would have been out of character for the star of Pearl, who doesn’t have much of a social media presence, if any. But the Instagram account that posted it, @miagoth_, had more than a million followers and was marked with a blue “verified” checkmark. Within days, the image racked up nearly 500,000 likes, including from peers in the entertainment industry, despite the page being labeled as a fan account. The image, as The Verge reported, was AI-generated, posted by an account Goth’s representative said they’d complained to Instagram about before for posting “counterfeit, AI images” of Goth. Meta allows users to purchase blue “verified” checkmarks, even if the account is not run by a prominent figure or isn’t an official page. “The fact that this fan account meets Instagram’s criteria to qualify for a ‘blue check’ is disconcerting on a fundamental level,” Christine Tripicchio, a representative for Goth, told The Verge in an email. “Beyond that, it is incomprehensible that Instagram evidently prioritizes the dissemination of forged and manipulated images over the protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Because of the news of her divorce, the post trickled through the celebrity gossip outlets, and that coverage in turn propagated the post through Google search. Searches for the actress and the shirt triggered an AI-generated overview saying Goth was taking “a clear swipe at her ex, Shia LaBeouf, following their recent divorce filing,” in turn citing the aforementioned blogs. A section in Google search results labeled “Mia Goth turns heads on Instagram by wearing a sassy ‘My ex is my biggest fan’ t-shirt” was featured prominently, along with links to social media posts discussing the image. Instagram eventually removed the account for impersonating a public figure. Since consumer generative AI tools became available several years ago, some of the more memorable — and controversial — use cases have involved famous people. The human subjects in question have historically not responded well to being digitally cloned and used as playthings: An AI-generated Drake sound-alike song was wiped from YouTube following copyright strikes. Scarlett Johansson hired a legal team after OpenAI released a voice for ChatGPT that sounded like her without her consent. Ariana Grande is said to have blocked an account posting AI-generated content of her last year. Taylor Swift publicly endorsed Kamala Harris for president in 2024, saying she was moved to clarify her position after Donald Trump posted fake images suggesting she endorsed him. There was a moment when everyone, even the rich and famous, was grappling with norms around a new technology. Now, the trough of AI content online is only growing — and it’s not clear if anyone is trying or able to stop it. AI content depicting female public figures is often overtly sexual. A profile that exclusively posts AI-generated images of Johansson — often with bare feet prominently displayed — included contact information so that companies could advertise on the account, along with links to Patreon and Telegram channels selling subscriptions. The content off-platform used Johansson’s name and (AI) image to advertise adult content. Another account posts realistic AI-generated images of actors and musicians like Millie Bobby Brown, Zendaya, and Grande, always partially undressed or in sexualized positions. Some accounts have their own niche, like “Stranger Things actors getting married to each other.” After The Verge asked Meta about eight accounts posting celebrity deepfake content, spokesperson Alex Dziedzan said the company had removed some of the accounts. Two of them — the Goth one and the Johansson one — appear to be taken down. “We do not permit accounts to use someone’s likeness to pose as that individual, regardless of whether the content is authentic or AI-generated,” Dziedzan said in an email. Taylor Swift is holding a drink, rapping along to Drake’s “Burning Bridges,” expletives and all. “I’m off a [Quaalude]/it make my body tingle,” she sings, wearing the dress from the fateful 2009 VMAs moment. The video is AI, obviously. It has 1.8 million views on Instagram. [Media: “I don’t think her pr team gonna like her saying the N word,” someone commented. Instagram is filled with videos like this, often inexplicably following very specific formats. A clip of AI Shrek doing the same thing as AI Swift has 3.1 million views. Here’s Steve Jobs, swaggering around to a different Drake song with a bottle of champagne in his hand (371,000 views). There’s also an identical Lionel Messi version (2.1 million views) posted by a different account. Here are Formula 1 drivers Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen lipsyncing to “APT” by Bruno Mars and Rosé (2.9 million views). Another clip shows AI Swift’s wedding to AI Travis Kelce at AI Madison Square Garden. “ai he wore white tuxedo,” one fan helpfully fact-checked. In the absence of national right of publicity laws, AI-generated content featuring real people is being litigated on the platform level. (The US’s Take It Down Act, which was signed into law in 2025, specifically criminalizes the distribution of nonconsensual intimate imagery, including AI-generated content, and compels platforms to remove it within 48 hours.) YouTube has likeness detection, perhaps the most robust deepfake monitoring and takedown system. Under the program, YouTube will scan its platform for visual matches for a person — and as of recently, sound-alikes — and allow them to request takedowns of content. Not every takedown request is accepted; the company says it considers public interest, newsworthiness, and consent in evaluating takedowns. The program was initially opened to public figures like celebrities, content creators, politicians, and journalists, but now covers every adult with a YouTube account. In the past, the company has said that the number of takedown requests it receives is relatively small. Creators want to be aware of what’s been posted of them on YouTube, but it often ends up being “fairly benign or additive to their overall business,” Amjad Hanif, vice president of creator products, said in a press briefing in March. YouTube spokesperson Jack Malon noted in an email to The Verge that the company’s likeness detection was developed in partnership with the entertainment industry. Malon said that in the first half of 2026, YouTube removed over 95 percent of the videos that were reported through the program for takedowns. AI-generated content on Meta platforms often has labels identifying it as such. Some content, like realistic videos of people or audio of AI-generated voices, is required to have an AI label. Still images, on the other hand, are exempt from the labeling requirement — meaning that the fake image of Mia Goth wouldn’t have required a disclosure under Meta’s rules. The company also introduced “AI-generated profile” labels that apply to an entire account where the avatar depicted doesn’t exist in the real world after an influx of AI influencer types flooded the platform. But there is a cottage industry of accounts that pump out AI-generated imagery of real people that the algorithm seems to like. Some of the content isn’t obviously nefarious, just kind of strange: There’s a genre on Facebook, for example, of AI-generated movie premiere videos where the original cast (in costume) walks the red carpet next to actors for a recast version. One profile advertises $29-per-month online courses on how to make money through AI content. AI-generated celebrity content also has the capacity to truly trick people into thinking it’s real, as in the case of the image (and account) depicting Goth. The specific post that went viral suggested the actress was taunting LaBeouf, who has been accused of abuse by another ex-partner and was filmed in 2015 saying he “would have killed [Goth]” if he had continued to argue with her. The fake image was attention-grabbing, shady, and timely — in other words, perfect for social media virality but a potential liability for the parties involved. The incident illustrates the failures of trust and safety provisions that are supposed to protect against this kind of confusion. On social media, AI content mingles freely with standard-issue reposts of real images. And even when one page is taken down, there are others that continue to push out content: Another Instagram account — still live — with over 300,000 followers posts a steady stream of pictures and videos of Johansson, which appear to be a mix of authentic images and AI-generated content. One of its most popular posts is what looks to be an AI image of Johansson with nearly half a million likes. There is no AI disclosure, in line with Meta’s rules. The deepfaked Johansson lies on a couch, bare feet displayed prominently. It is not her, obviously — but her fans in the comments either don’t know or don’t care.

articles.title: Google’s Universal Cart shopping tool launches in the US
articles.summary: The new shopping tool is available in the U.S. across Google Search and the Gemini app.
articles.body:
Google on Thursday said “Universal Cart,” a tool that lets users collect and monitor products they find across search and in the Gemini app, is now available to U.S. users. The company first previewed the tool at Google I/O in May.

The idea is to make online shopping easier to manage. Find something you like, save it to your cart, and move on. When you return later, your items and shopping progress are still there, so you don’t have to hunt down the same products or start over. Universal Cart can collect items from multiple retailers, turning it into a central hub for browsing and keeping track of potential purchases.

Google says the cart can also help shoppers stay on top of deals and availability. The tool can send notifications when a saved product’s price drops or when an out-of-stock item becomes available again.

The tool is also designed to offer more tailored help during the shopping process. Google says it can take credit card perks into account when helping users choose how to pay, and also surface relevant promo codes.

Checkout is tied to Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol, or UCP, an open standard the company introduced earlier this year. UCP is designed to help AI agents and retailers work together across different parts of the shopping journey, including checkout.

Google is already deeply invested in AI-powered shopping, and Universal Cart is its latest effort to make the experience more convenient. It joins features such as conversational product discovery in Search’s AI Mode and Google’s “Let Google Call” tool, which uses an AI agent to contact nearby stores and check whether an item is in stock.

Google isn’t the only company bringing AI into e-commerce. Amazon , OpenAI , and other rivals have added agentic commerce features as companies look for ways to make chatbots useful beyond answering questions.

articles.title: How Windows is being optimized for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops
articles.summary: Microsoft has focused on local AI models, gaming, and memory management.
articles.body: Microsoft and Nvidia held a launch party for the first wave of RTX Spark laptops last week in San Francisco, where a new wave of AI PCs took center stage amid a packed crowd and a lively hands-on area. A day after the media event, I was invited to a quieter Nvidia event to hear a lot more about the new RTX Spark computing platform. While Nvidia’s new laptops might look like regular Windows machines, the chips inside are Arm-based, instead of the traditional x64 architecture used by AMD and Intel. Combined with a powerful GPU, RTX Spark is designed for the future of AI, and it means a lot of work has gone into getting these laptops ready for launch. One of the biggest challenges was getting Windows ready for AI agents and local AI models. The big selling point of RTX Spark is the combination of Arm CPU, Blackwell GPU, and unified memory to enable powerful AI models to run on a laptop, so the experience of setting up an AI agent needs to be quick and easy. “When users get into Windows for the first time, they’ll see a new Get Started experience that will launch on an RTX Spark laptop that allows them to find the agent they want, get started with that agent, install it, and get to that agent in only two clicks,” says Peter Dawoud, principal program manager at Microsoft. Agents can be installed and updated through the Windows Store, so you don’t have to worry about finding updates or figuring out what dependencies each one needs. “We’ll continue to develop it and add more features so that agents can offer a whole new bunch of experiences coming through Windows,” Dawoud says. Hermes, Perplexity, and OpenClaw are the first three officially supported agents in Windows at the launch of RTX Spark, but Microsoft is working on bringing others on board. That will presumably eventually include Muse, which Meta announced last week is coming to Windows at some point in the future. Getting started with Hermes was mostly a two-click experience in my testing, but I did run into trouble getting OpenClaw set up properly. The app kept complaining that a local gateway hadn’t been installed properly, and it took an uninstall and reinstall to get everything working fully. I’ve been using OpenClaw for a variety of tasks over the past week, but it’s going to take a lot more testing to really understand the value of this local AI support beyond obvious tasks like coding. Powerful as the RTX Spark chip is, large local models are still a lot slower at responding to prompts than cloud models, so I get the feeling that I’ll use this more for tasks I want to run overnight or leave processing in the background. Microsoft has also done a lot of work behind the scenes to optimize Nvidia’s RTX Spark chips for all the things you’d expect to do on a Windows laptop. Unlike an Intel or AMD laptop, RTX Spark laptops make use of Microsoft’s Prism emulator for apps that don’t have a native Arm version. Emulation was a problem on Windows on Arm for more than a decade, but the launch of Qualcomm’s first Snapdragon X series laptops a couple of years ago has helped RTX Spark laptops now benefit from a variety of Arm-native apps and Microsoft’s improved emulator. There’s still a lot of tweaking required for Nvidia’s new chips, though. “Emulation isn’t generic. Each platform needs tuning,” says Dawoud. ”Each core is different. How we translate x64 to that core needs to be highly optimized, and for RTX Spark we’ve done a lot of work to optimize for its microarchitecture.” Some of that optimization has been focused on gaming, particularly because CPUs often dictate frame pacing of games and how smooth they feel, while a GPU does the heavy lifting of rendering the game. Microsoft is quietly shipping Prism updates all the time. “Every month we ship an update to improve compatibility,” says Dawoud. “It’s something we’re constantly working on at the Windows team.” Microsoft has been focused on memory optimization for RTX Spark laptops, too. Microsoft’s own Surface Laptop Ultra can ship with up to 128GB of unified memory, making it possible to load huge models into memory. “We made incredible investments in Unified Memory Architecture to enable you to load as much as possible into the 128GB,” says Dawoud. “But we are also conserving a little bit of space to make sure the system maintains its responsiveness, and the applications running on top of Windows continue to run well and continue to be responsive.” Microsoft has completed optimizations for how memory works on RTX Spark, including tuning for power and performance, maximizing battery life, and ensuring that you can run a game while rendering a video in the background. You can even manually adjust how much of the unified memory is dedicated to the GPU side with a slider in Nvidia’s Windows app. This slider is useful if you have an RTX Spark laptop with 24GB or 32GB of memory, so you can balance more to the GPU for particular apps and games. While Microsoft and Nvidia maintain that RTX Spark laptops shouldn’t be considered gaming machines, they’re more than capable of running the latest AAA titles. “Nvidia and Microsoft have expended a lot of energy over the last many, many, many, many months trying to think deeply about making sure that RTX Spark can deliver a true form of RTX gaming experience,” says Dawoud. One of the first parts of making sure RTX Spark supports gaming was getting anti-cheat vendors on board with Windows on Arm. Some of that work started with Qualcomm, but it has clearly accelerated with Nvidia’s involvement. Fortnite, Marvel Rivals, Arc Raiders, Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and many other games that have anti-cheat engines will be supported out of the box on RTX Spark laptops. Nvidia and Microsoft are also working with a variety of other anti-cheat providers to make more games available in the future. Activision’s Ricochet anti-cheat engine, used in Call of Duty, will support RTX Spark at some point in 2027, and EA has committed to getting its Javelin anti-cheat working in Battlefield in early 2027. PUBG will start working on RTX Spark laptops in the first half of 2027, and Riot Games has committed to getting League of Legends and Valorant running on RTX Spark laptops at some point in the future. Microsoft is also bringing its advanced shader delivery system to RTX Spark. This allows the Xbox app to preload game shaders during download. It’s the same experience that’s been available on Xbox Ally devices, allowing you to download a game, click launch, and have shaders automatically precompiled so you don’t have to sit there and wait to play. I haven’t run into many game compatibility issues during my testing, even though nearly every game I’ve tested has run emulated. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips just weren’t powerful enough on the GPU side to make gaming a reality, but Nvidia has put a much more powerful GPU inside the RTX Spark. Your mileage in gaming is going to vary depending on the title, but for the most part I’ve found that medium settings, running at 1440p and DLSS performance, will get you to a stable 60fps in most games. In some titles you may need to drop the resolution or settings lower, though. This definitely isn’t as good as a dedicated gaming laptop, but for something that’s roughly on the level of a MacBook Pro it’s more than good enough for gaming on the go. The last part of Microsoft’s work on RTX Spark involves Windows features. Surprisingly, Copilot Plus PC features like Recall aren’t available on RTX Spark devices at launch. It’s not clear why they’re delayed, but it sounds like they won’t be available fully until next year. “We are partnering closely with Nvidia to deliver Copilot Plus PC experiences on RTX Spark, expected to first become available to Windows Insiders later this year,” says Adrienne Brewbaker, senior director of Windows marketing. Microsoft is also working on a new Windows Search interface that may work best on devices like the RTX Spark. The interface is being overhauled to focus on speed, and even includes actions that let you do things like turn Bluetooth on or off right from the search bar. It essentially turns Windows Search into a launcher, a much-needed improvement. “We think you’ll love it,” says Dawoud. “We think it’ll change the way people interact with Windows.” The pad * Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports. Retro gaming is booming at the moment thanks to decompilations and recompilations that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft is leaning into this effort with a new Xbox Labs group that’s a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,” according to Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.” Part of this also seems to be about using AI inside Xbox, as Sharma notes games share many of the same properties as the workloads AI agents have been tackling on the coding side of things. * Microsoft has a new machine learning tool to improve weather forecasts. Microsoft claims to have solved old-school physics-based weather forecasting with machine learning. Researchers at the company say they’ve found a new, cost-effective way to make weather forecasts more accurate two to six weeks in advance. Microsoft has even open-sourced the tool it’s using, and published the findings in the journal Nature. * Honey, Xbox shrunk its controller. Microsoft surprised everyone this week with some new Xbox hardware. The Xbox Nano controller is the company’s smallest controller yet, designed for younger players, smaller hands, and gaming on the go. At $49.99, it’s also more affordable than the regular Xbox controller. It’s around five inches in length and includes Xbox wireless and Bluetooth support for connecting to Xbox consoles and phones, tablets, and PCs. The Xbox Nano controller also includes a rechargeable battery, and doesn’t require AA batteries or a separate charging pack like most Xbox controllers. You can preorder the Xbox Nano now, and it will start shipping in November. * Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs. Microsoft announced its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip this week, and it’s not all about beating Amazon or Google anymore. This time around the Maia 300 improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, and it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. These advances will soon make Maia the “primary AI interference system” for Microsoft’s products and services, making the company less reliant on GPUs from Nvidia and AMD. * Satya Nadella says we should assume all AI models are “compromised.” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella published a lengthy post on X over the weekend that laid out his views on the dangers of advanced AI models. Nadella says we can no longer accept a world where AI is treated as a “set of nested black boxes” whose advice and actions we simply accept or reject. He calls for building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leave behind “tamper-proof human readable evidence.” Nadella’s recommendations are thoughtful and well-balanced, but unfortunately they were overshadowed by his use of “Super Intelligence” instead of AI. That’s what President Donald Trump wants companies to call AI, and it seems Microsoft is towing the line. * Microsoft launches its new AI model for making decisions quickly. Microsoft has announced its new Microsoft-Decision-1 model just days after OpenAI revealed its new Decisions API. The model is designed to choose the most efficient AI model to complete a task, and Microsoft claims it beats others in tests to determine speed and accuracy. * Microsoft 365 Family subscribers will finally be able to share AI benefits. Microsoft is about to let Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers share Copilot and AI usage features, alongside access to Office apps and OneDrive storage, with up to five other people on a plan. The bad part? Instead of getting 1TB of OneDrive storage per account, Microsoft is now limiting this to just 2TB of shared storage across the entire plan. Microsoft argues this makes storage more flexible if one member exceeds 1TB, but it looks like it’s an easy way for the company to upsell more OneDrive storage in reality. * Forza Horizon 6 is being delayed on PS5 to January 2027. I reported last month that Forza Horizon 6’s PS5 release would be delayed to early 2027, and now Playground Games has officially confirmed the game will debut on January 26th. The delay means the PS5 version will now coincide with a new expansion for the game. Playground Games will also sell a Premium Edition of Forza Horizon 6 on PS5 that offers up to five days of early access ahead of January 26th. * Microsoft and Japan took down a cybercrime network behind over a billion scam messages. Hopefully you’ll start seeing fewer scam texts about parking fines or fake deliveries, as Microsoft says it has helped dismantle a marketplace for scammers. Together with Japan’s National Police Agency, Microsoft tracked scam activity back to a marketplace called YAM Store and some phishing kits that helped scammers send messages. Microsoft says it disabled over 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and blocked over 100,000 web domains being used for impersonation and fraud. * The Link to Windows app for Android might soon let you shut down your PC remotely. You can already lock your Windows PC through the Link to Windows app, but it looks like you’ll soon be able to shut it down remotely, too. An updated beta version has a new power menu with options to lock, sleep, shut down, or restart a PC. * How Gears of War: E-Day solves the Xbox Series S memory issue by tapping the SSD. The Coalition has created a solution for working around the 10GB of memory limit on Microsoft’s smaller Xbox Series S console. We’ve heard plenty of stories over the years about how this memory limit has been difficult at times for developers, and now a bespoke system designed in collaboration with the Xbox platform team and Advanced Technology Group has allowed E-Day to use the SSD as a new tier of memory. The technique has allowed The Coalition to keep the game’s density high on the Series S, instead of lowering the quality. * Microsoft’s science president is leaving after 16 years. There are few people who have had such an impact inside Microsoft as Peter Lee.The president of Microsoft Science is resigning for a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to join an elite team,” in what he says is a “major detour” from the work he has been doing over the past 20 years. Lee has always been the main face of Microsoft Research, and he led the company’s research operations across 14 worldwide laboratories over the past four years. I’m not sure where this leaves Microsoft Research, but it definitely leaves Microsoft without another talented executive. I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else.
