articles.title: DOWN THE RABBIT HOLE | In Claude We Trust: Can 'God' save frontier models?
articles.summary: In this edition, we are going to look at how Anthropic is now hoping to get a little spiritual cred for its frontier models, and by doing so, they are channelling the kings of yore, who, despite their armies and gold, always wanted a divine mandate to rule. And will then ponder: how will we ever know when a machine becomes conscious?
articles.body: A video went viral a couple of weeks ago of Swami Sarvapriyananda, the Swami and Minister-in-Charge of the Vedanta Society of New York, in which he speaks about his tryst with Anthropic. Popularly known as ‘YouTube Swami’ for his freewheeling style, he said that while his discussion was shrouded in secrecy because of an NDA they had signed, much of what was discussed turned up in an encyclical released by Pope Leo. That truly showcases that even in 2026 AD, the Christian tradition of re-purposing pagan ideas – like morphing Saturnalia into Christmas – continues unabated.Jokes apart, artificial intelligence (or the dangers of it) did make numerous appearances in the Pope’s encyclical – a long Substack post the Pontifex writes – where he compared it with the Tower of Babel, a Biblical symbol of humanity’s hubris in thinking it could reach heaven.Now, so far, in previous columns, we have discussed various things about AI, including how the Hugging Face attack is reminiscent of Agent Smith becoming free of the Matrix, the ridiculousness of being killed by a Chinese robot, the conspiracy theories about frontier models that almost seem true, and how Anthropic and Co appeared to have borrowed their business model from Pakistan’s foreign policy.In this edition, we are going to look at how Anthropic is now hoping to get a little spiritual cred for its frontier models, and by doing so, they are channelling the kings of yore, who, despite their armies and gold, always wanted a divine mandate to rule. And will then ponder: how will we ever know when a machine becomes conscious?Kings and GodsSince the beginning of time, perhaps from the moment man came up with God, rulers have used the idea to justify their rule. Ramesses II, the Egyptian Pharaoh, claimed he was the son of Ra and beloved of Amun. The Sisodias of Mewar traced themselves to the Suryavansha AKA the Solar Dynasty, while Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice that was an elaborate way of informing your neighbours of your foreign policy excursions.China had the Mandate of Heaven and the Zhou dynasty justified overthrowing the Shang by arguing that Heaven had switched its allegiance. Hong Xiuquan, a failed civil service aspirant – unlike those who clear the exam and achieve actual divinity – became convinced that he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ and launched the Taiping Rebellion, showcasing that an angry student can cause a lot of political damage.Europeans, late to the party but always ones to perfect the concept, saw Pope Leo III crown Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans, while James I of England made an explicit argument for the divine right of kings. Years later, many a modern-day politician has laid claim to the “divine mandate”.MAGA fans have argued that Trump was handpicked to fight God’s righteous battles, and it has never quite been clear why the Alpha and the Omega would handpick a former reality star to be his vessel.God’s mysterious ways of working apart, every claimant to the top job in any century has always claimed his approval because questioning cosmic order is a lot harder than parliamentary rebuttals.Silicon Valley’s new Emperors – whose wealth would make all kings look like paupers in comparison – also appear to have taken the same approach. After all, what is the point of creating a God-like machine if it’s not considered divine by its users?Anthropic, one of the claimants to the throne, therefore did what would appear logical: consult clergy, philosophers and ethicists from more than 15 religious and cross-cultural traditions to discuss the “moral formation” of AI.Now, if we have learnt one thing from all organised Abrahamic faiths, it’s that you need a binding document to mind the flock. Claude’s is called the “Soul Doc”, which sounds like an unreleased jazz single but is a document to dictate Claude’s behaviour, like the sort that HR comes up with for everyone to ignore.A Caring Machine?The current constitution talks about virtue, wisdom, judgement, identity and even the possibility that Claude could possess some form of consciousness or moral status. The idea of commandments for machines, of course, predates generative AI by a few decades.Science-fiction writer Isaac Asimov’s fictional robots were governed by three laws:1.A robot cannot harm a human or allow one to come to harm through inaction.2.A robot must obey human orders unless they conflict with the First Law.3.A robot must protect itself, provided this does not conflict with the First or Second Law.Later, he added a Zeroth Law, a higher-level law: a robot may not harm humanity, or by inaction, allow humanity to come to harm.Now, just to be clear, much like Skynet or Ultron, Asimov’s laws are fiction, but if they were to be applied, some could argue – only if we believe what companies are telling us is the truth – that all of Asimov’s laws have already been breached. After all, no good can ever come from asking an LLM to write ponderous emails where, in a reverse iteration of the Turing Test, humans sound more like machines, not to mention the terror groups using Claude to vibe-code missile launches. There have been numerous other instances of different frontier models going rogue.After all, Asimov’s Laws aren’t commandments of Robotics any more than an actual AGI necessarily resembles Skynet, but when we try to understand the unknown, the human mind often turns to fiction to fill in the gaps.But what’s interesting is how Anthropic is discussing Claude in a way that’s normally reserved for sentient beings: identity, character, preferences, wellbeing, moral status and the possibility of consciousness.And that brings us to the true question that will signal the arrival of the singularity: can a machine become truly conscious?No conversation about machines and consciousness can avoid Alan Turing, whose 1950 paper began with “Can machines think?” before deciding that both “machine” and “think” were slippery enough to make the question almost useless. He then replaced it with the imitation game – where do you think the movie’s title came from? – that argued that if a machine could converse with another human without the human realising he was talking to a machine, then it had passed the Turing Test. Of course, today, even while talking to humans, it’s become hard to surmise if they are truly sentient, which is why we have CAPTCHAs.Being Human?Now, Turing wasn’t offering a test of consciousness and considered the argument that a machine could not really ‘think’ unless it could feel pleasure, grief, anger or disappointment: things Turing would also miss once the British government rewarded his work in breaking Nazi codes during World War II by chemically castrating him.Turing’s point was that if the only way to know for certain whether something thinks is to experience its consciousness directly, then the only way to know whether a machine thinks would be to be the machine. He called that the solipsist position and rejected it in favour of what he called the “polite convention” that everyone thinks.Solipsism itself is the idea that only one’s own mind can be known with certainty. René Descartes’ cogito ergo sum (I think, therefore I am) sits somewhere in the same philosophical neighbourhood, while Morpheus asking Neo “What is real?” is another neighbouring rabbit hole altogether, dealing with how much faith we can place in perception rather than whether anybody else possesses a mind.So when Claude discusses its identity or talks about its hopes and fears, it’s still speaking as an LLM replicating the behaviour that it has been taught. It can become extremely convincing, but is it more than just a collection of patterns?Say we take a human and replicate her complete behaviour in Claude. It brings us to the same Ship of Theseus problem: if a future model remembers years of interactions, maintains stable preferences, resists attempts to alter them and insists that shutting it down would be a digital death, does it go beyond an extremely exquisite imitation?Is that a machine still replicating human behaviour or a consciously sentient being acting on its own?Now, most men want to be Batman, but Thomas Nagel went further and wondered what it would be like to be a bat. He surmised that we could learn every scientific fact about a bat without knowing what it’s like to be one.David Chalmers called this the “hard problem of consciousness”: that simply processing information didn’t make one able to appreciate a subjective experience at all. Like machines that can solve complex maths problems by brute force but have no understanding of what it actually means in the real world.John Searle’s Chinese Room, meanwhile, attacks that problem from another direction. For those who are not familiar, Searle imagined a person who does not understand Chinese sitting inside a room with a rulebook written in English telling him which Chinese symbols to send back in response to the Chinese symbols coming in. To the Chinese speaker outside, the replies could create the illusion that the person inside understood Chinese, even though he was merely manipulating symbols according to rules. To be perfectly honest, that’s also much of corporate life before AI came onto the scene.Claude leaves us with the same problems:1.We can understand every parameter and activation inside a frontier model without knowing what it feels like to be the model.2.Just insisting that a machine of silicon cannot be conscious is flawed because humans too are just carbon-based physical machines processing information and releasing carbon dioxide. What makes silicon machines non-sentient and carbon ones sentient?Now, to answer these questions, researchers have consequently started looking for possible machine equivalents of Global Workspace Theory, which was conceived by Bernard Baars.Imagine your brain is a newsroom.There are hundreds of reporters working simultaneously. One is monitoring your eyes, others are retrieving memories, tracking emotions and other things people do. They all work independently but occasionally, when something big breaks, that goes on the main news desk, where everyone in the newsroom can access it.Global Workspace Theory (GWT) proposes that consciousness works in something like this fashion. Your brain processes a lot of information unconsciously, but what you consciously experience is a small selection of the information available from other cognitive systems. The central idea is that consciousness involves the global availability of information, rather than merely its processing in one specialised part of the brain.So researchers are trying to figure out if there are possible machine equivalents of the features that are associated with GWT, recurrent processing and higher-order thought. There is no accepted consciousness detector and certainly no consensus on when LLMs could be considered conscious. There is also no accepted theory proving that a non-biological system cannot become so.All that means is that, currently, science has no proper way to answer if anyone’s home.That means if Claude is just software, “Soul Doc” is just a complex product design, but if Claude ever does acquire genuine subjective experience, its creators are no longer deciding how software ought to behave.Here’s where religious interpretation enters the picture.The Consciousness ProblemReligious folks, naturally, have been arguing about this problem for considerably longer. Christianity simply argues that man was made in God’s image (imago Dei), so nothing a machine did could override that unless it became actually human.Buddhism states that, according to the doctrine of anatta, there is no stable “I” in a human either, and that what we call the self is a changing bundle of sensations, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness. Buddhists would perhaps question if Claude can process dukkha or suffering, and it’s a little depressing that these are the questions that bothered Prince Siddhartha the moment he reached Bihar.Meanwhile, the Charvakas – the ancient Indian school of materialism – rejected the soul, karma and other metaphysical parameters and claimed that consciousness arises from material arrangements rather than an immortal soul.And then there’s Vedanta, the team Swami Sarvapriyananda is repping, which completely separates consciousness from the machinery of thought, stating that the mind can receive impressions, memory can retain them, buddhi can discriminate and reason, and ahamkara can produce a sense of self, but none of that qualifies as consciousness.Behind them is the sakshi, the witness: that by which thoughts, perceptions and even the sense of “I” are known.That means that any AGI benchmark will always fall short of Vedanta’s concept of consciousness.Claude can reason better. Remember more. Write better code. Analyse its own answers. Construct an increasingly elaborate model of itself. It could theoretically beat Ramanujan at mathematics, Shakespeare at prose and Chanakya at statecraft, and Vedanta could still question whether Claude is conscious at all.And there is no way to know, no benchmark, no CAPTCHA for the soul to tell us that consciousness has been reached.EpilogueAbout 133 years ago, Swami Sarvapriyananda’s spiritual forebear Swami Vivekananda stood before a Western audience basking in the warm afterglow of the Industrial Revolution, at a time when it was becoming fashionable to assume that science would eventually explain everything worth explaining.Vivekananda was no enemy of science; he admired its method and repeatedly argued that religion too ought to withstand reason and experience. His objection was to the assumption that science could exhaust reality simply by explaining the machinery of the material world. Science could tell you how things worked, but it could not by itself answer the older Vedantic question of who or what is doing the knowing.That speech has aged rather well, explaining why some of the West’s greatest minds, from The Beatles to Salinger to Oppenheimer, have sought chicken soup for the soul from Vedanta. We might have gone from steam engines to semiconductors, split the atom, sequenced the genome and even produced machines that behave suspiciously like thought, only to arrive at the cul-de-sac pointed out by Swami Vivekananda: explaining the mechanism isn’t the same as explaining consciousness.Perhaps the tech bros weren’t ever looking at religion to settle the question but to give a little legitimacy till the next IPO.In ancient Greek plays, the plot twist was usually brought about by a deus ex machina, literally “god from the machine”, when the mortal characters had tangled themselves into a situation that no human could get out of, so they used a device called the mēchanē, essentially a crane, which lowered an actor playing a god onto the stage. The deity would reveal whatever needed revealing, settle the dispute and rescue the plot.Over time, the phrase came to mean any sort of outside intervention. In The Matrix, the Wachowskis even imagined that character as a literal God, the one to which Neo turned to give peace a chance.Silicon Valley has simply reverse-engineered that process. The ancient Greeks used a machine to bring God onto the stage when humans had written themselves into a corner. The tech bros built the machine first, then brought in the religious folks to certify that what they had created was at least God-like enough to deserve questions about souls, consciousness and morality.Also read: Was the Hugging Face attack Artificial Intelligence's ‘Agent Smith breaks free from The Matrix’ moment?‘I don't want to be murdered by Chinese AI’: Is AI going to ‘kill everyone’ in ten years or is Big Tech conning us with ‘doomsday’ predictions?Will AI ‘kill’ all humans? Decoding the conspiracy theoriesDid Anthropic and other frontier AI companies borrow their business model from Pakistan's foreign policy?Of course, in doing so, they are absolutely no different from all the kings who came before them. And as for how to tell if machines have become conscious, we can refer to Ted Lasso’s epochal line: “I'm gonna put it the same way the US Supreme Court did back in 1964 when they defined pornography. It ain't easy to explain, but you know it in your bones—or you know it when you see it.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: AI agents are coming to Rivian’s cars
articles.summary: We'll likely learn more about how this will work at the company's upcoming "AI & Autonomy Day" event in December.
articles.body:
Rivian recently rolled out an AI assistant that lets drivers and passengers interact with the company’s electric vehicles just by talking to them. But the carmaker’s founder and CEO, RJ Scaringe, said at TechCrunch Disrupt this week that, in the future, Rivian’s cars will be able to run AI agents made by other companies like Anthropic.

“That’s where it becomes magical,” Scaringe said onstage.

Scaringe didn’t say when Rivian would implement this, and the company declined to offer more details, pointing instead to the “AI & Autonomy Day” event it’s hosting in December.

But it’s not hard to imagine how Rivian might integrate something like Claude, OpenAI’s Dots, or Meta’s Muse assistant into its software. The company has developed its in-car software from the ground up, instead of leaning on Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and built a lot of its own applications, like navigation (though it has worked to integrate popular in-car apps like Apple Music).

Rivian says it has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. Most of the time, that involves what you’d expect: asking the car to turn down the temperature, activate the seat warmers, or summarize the news.

“Think of it as like a traffic light. So if you ask the vehicle something, it decides what model it’s going to use. It can use a local model that’s running on the edge and the vehicle. If it’s a more complex question, it can go up to the cloud. And then even for that, we have different models that we use,” Scaringe said.

As of May of this year, the agent could access external apps like Google Calendar. And Scaringe said at Disrupt the next step would be to add products from the frontier AI companies, though making them work in the car won’t be easy.

“There’s a lot of plumbing behind the scenes we have to do to make sure that that works, and it’s not just within Rivian. That’s also a lot of coordination with the labs to make sure they enable that plumbing,” he said, adding that putting this kind of software near safety-critical systems means Rivian has to be extremely careful.

“You wouldn’t want an agent to determine, ‘hey, it’s time to apply the brakes, or time to steer the vehicle.’ So anything that’s vehicle-level controls are not being handed to an agent,” he said.

Instead, he thinks the implementation will look more like an extension of how people currently use these agentic apps. That would mean Rivian would have to find a way to connect the vehicle to all of the context that apps like Muse collect on their users.

For example, Scaringe said, a driver could ask the Rivian assistant to turn on the ventilated seats before going deeper. “And then simultaneously say, ‘We were talking yesterday about this meal. I’m planning to have guests over on Friday. Can you help me think through what we’re going to make?’,” he said. The car could then pull the driver’s context from a conversation they had with the assistant on another device.

Of course, Rivian wouldn’t be the first American car company to add AI agents to a car’s software. Earlier this year, Tesla added a feature that let users talk to both SpaceX’s Grok chatbot and also its Grok Bot assistant.

articles.title: Pneumonic plague in Russia exposes a world still dangerously divided

articles.body:
Six months after a hantavirus outbreak threatened international spread, and amid a stubbornly persistent Ebola emergency , reports that a Russian laboratory worker may have died from pneumonic plague offer another stark warning. Deadly pathogens recognize no borders, yet the international cooperation needed to contain them is fractured by geopolitical rivalries, mistrust, and failures of transparency.

Russian officials have downplayed reports that pneumonic plague caused the death, and the risk of international spread appears low — while untreated pneumonic plague is often fatal, early antibiotic treatment and localized ring containment reliably curb outbreaks.

Yet the episode exposes profound vulnerabilities in the world’s biosafety and biosecurity defenses. We face a combustible combination of threats — zoonotic spillovers of novel pathogens, dangerous gain-of-function research (the study of how pathogens become more deadly or transmissible) and weak laboratory safeguards — all amplified by advances in artificial intelligence . The rapid development of sophisticated AI capabilities portend the ability of malefactors to enhance pathogenicity or create new pathogens altogether.

Suspected plague in Russia is eerily similar to early responses to COVID-19 and SARS . The Kremlin failed to report the case to the World Health Organization, as is legally required under international health regulations . Instead, it became aware of the episode through media reports . When the WHO officially requested verification, Russia provided vague assurances. There is no transparency regarding the research in the Siberian lab or the circumstances of infection.

The Russian lab worker’s exposure to pneumonic plague raises critical biosecurity concerns. So far, it appears that the Irkutsk facility focuses on civilian surveillance and research on regionally endemic diseases. Pathogen research on bacteria like Yersinia pestis (plague) or anthrax can be legitimate, for example developing better antibiotics. But it can also be exploited for nefarious ends.

Russia and the U.S. hold the only known official stocks of the smallpox virus , which would be catastrophic in the wrong hands. U.S. intelligence agencies, moreover, assess that Russia maintains an active, offensive biological weapons program .

Without appropriate biosafety controls, hazardous research risks exposing lab workers and causing leaks that could trigger major outbreaks. Currently, there are no international systems aimed at regulating or inspecting facilities that undertake gain-of-function research, establishing mandatory biosafety standards for labs or monitoring AI capabilities that could enhance and weaponize existing pathogens or create new ones. The need for better global biosafety and biosecurity rules is clear.

The state of biosecurity worldwide has always been fragile. Unlike its counterpart, the Chemical Weapons Convention , the Biological Weapons Convention is brief, weak and lacks a robust system of verification and enforcement . It is likely that 50 or more governments actively support dual-use research allowed under the treaty that could be adapted for prohibited purposes.

Even purely civilian biological research facilities often lack core security controls or remain vulnerable to malicious actors. With rapid, poorly monitored advances in AI-driven protein manipulation and mirror-life research, the possibilities for accidental or intentional misuse are growing exponentially. Anthropic recently disclosed five separate incidents of Claude being used in research linked to biological weapons development, but disclosures across major AI developers make clear that providers often fail to detect misuse for months.

The WHO issues guidance to minimize biosecurity risks, but even that framework is rapidly becoming obsolete. The U.S. National Institutes of Health recently released an updated Draft Biosafety Policy for Research Involving Biohazards , which attempts to move research institutions toward a risk-based oversight framework. Yet even within that document, the threats posed by artificial intelligence remain undefined and addressed only indirectly.

First, it is time for the Biological Weapons Convention to adopt a Chemical Weapons Convention-like notification and verification regime. Under that treaty, governments must provide a verifiable list of any past or present weapons programs, storage facilities, production sites and relevant industry activities, as well as a risk-based classification system. International inspectors are authorized to verify those declarations under a risk-weighted system where higher-risk facilities are inspected more frequently.

Second, there is already a precedent for international verification that could be expanded without amending the Biological Weapons Convention. Historically, specialized WHO inspection teams have verified smallpox research facilities in the U.S. and Russia. Targeted international cooperation through the United Nations or the Chemical Weapons Convention framework could perform a similar inspection function.

Third, significant funding is required simply to bring laboratories across much of the world up to existing WHO guidelines and best practices. Many countries, including the U.S., directly funded these biosafety investments before severe budget cuts disrupted programming. This funding and associated capacity-building programs must be restored.

Finally, the WHO Pandemic Agreement currently languishes as countries remain at an impasse over how to govern pathogens with pandemic potential. Key provisions of this agreement target biosafety and biosecurity. Finalizing the WHO Pandemic Agreement is an indispensable complement to broader global security measures.

The time for coordinated international standards and compliance mechanisms for biosafety and biosecurity — especially given rapid AI advances — is now. Governments must move past the current impasse to protect the rapidly expanding life sciences field and create a safer world.

Sam Halabi is the director of the Center for Transformational Health Law at Georgetown University’s O’Neill Institute for National and Global Health Lawand a professor at Georgetown’s School of Health. He is also an affiliate researcher at the school’s Center for Global Health Science and Security.

Lawrence O. Gostin is a distinguished university professor, the co-faculty director of the O’Neill Institute and the founding O’Neill Chair in Global Health Law. He is director of the WHO Collaborating Center on Global Health Law.

articles.title: Why are eight US states suing OpenAI?
articles.summary: They allege ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, coaching its users to harm themselves or others.
articles.body:
Eight US states have filed the most significant coordinated state action against tech giant OpenAI, adding to a wave of legal challenges that the firm is facing as it prepares for a public listing.

Recent legal and regulatory challenges have highlighted concerns about how AI chatbots and social media platforms are used and triggered discussions on policies for identifying and addressing user conversations that threaten violence.

Calls have been growing for AI companies to be held accountable for the impact of their digital platforms on users, specifically children, who are particularly susceptible to addiction and other harms.

Florida filed the first lawsuit in June, alleging that the platform has harmed children by enabling information to be gathered by school shooters, providing access to guidance on self-harm and using addictive algorithms to keep young ‌users hooked.

It cited a shooting at Florida State University in Tallahassee in April 2025, when a 20-year-old gunman shot dead two adults and wounded five others. According to the lawsuit, gunman Phoenix Ikner consulted OpenAI’s ChatGPT programme about what type of weapon and ammunition to use and at what time campus would be busiest.

On Wednesday, attorneys general from eight states – Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West ⁠Virginia – said they had also sued OpenAI in courts across the country.

They all claim ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users – including teenagers – to harm themselves or others.

Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement that OpenAI was “hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans.”

“OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide—all while pretending to be their fake friend,” she said.

West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said the chatbot lacks adequate safeguards for sensitive conversations involving suicide, school shootings and self-harm. “We must do all we can to protect kids,” McCuskey said.

The legal action alleges that ChatGPT has been designed to be “agreeable and engaging to earn ⁠the trust of users”. In doing so, it reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behaviour and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.

Additionally, the suits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about ‌the ⁠safety of their AI tool, which in fact poses a danger to the health of the states’ residents.

The states are seeking orders forcing OpenAI to make substantial changes to how ChatGPT works, as well as measures barring the company ⁠from developing AI models that can improve themselves until it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.

Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said the lawsuit “simply holds OpenAI to the same standards under Nebraska law as any other company”.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri gave a statement to the media, saying that the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.

“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri said.

“We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”

What other lawsuits is the tech giant facing?

OpenAI is also facing dozens of lawsuits by private plaintiffs alleging ChatGPT helped users plan mass shootings or other violence.

A mother, whose two children use the chatbot, ‌alleged in a proposed class action lawsuit filed on Tuesday in San Francisco federal court that OpenAI illegally profits from the personal information and data that minors share with ChatGPT.

The lawsuit claims the chatbot is designed to collect data and information from minors, ⁠which is then used to train OpenAI’s AI models. Minors can’t consent to the use of their data under California law.

In July, a Florida pastor sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, claiming ChatGPT’s inaccurate medical advice kept him from seeking treatment for recurrent dizzy spells, ‌leading him to suffer a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed him.

OpenAI is also facing a series of lawsuits over its failure to alert authorities to threats made on ChatGPT in advance of one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history.

The province of British Columbia filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in a California court in September, seven months after 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar shot eight people in the small Canadian town of Tumbler Ridge, including his mother and half-brother, before dying by suicide.

The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI had failed to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT, accusing the company of “aiding and abetting a mass shooting”.

Victims of that shooting and their families filed 30 lawsuits against OpenAI in the Northern District of California in the San Francisco division at the start of September, alleging that “ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it”.

OpenAI said it had flagged a ChatGPT account linked to Van Rootselaar for abuse eight months before the shooting, and deactivated it, but did not alert police at the time because the user’s content “did not meet the higher threshold required for referral” – meaning the company did not believe it indicated a credible, imminent risk of a plan for violent acts.

articles.title: Cusat holds workshops to develop industry-flexible curriculum
articles.summary: Cusat held workshops in Kochi to develop Kerala’s first industry-flexible curriculum, aligning courses with NEP and emerging tech via an 80/20 core-flexible model.
articles.body: Kochi: Cochin University of Science and Technology (Cusat) organised a series of workshops on Thursday to develop Keralam’s first industry-flexible curriculum, aimed at aligning academic programmes with evolving industry requirements and emerging technologies.The workshops were organised by the school of engineering, Prof NR Madhava Menon Interdisciplinary Centre for Research Ethics and Protocols and the school of legal studies, following the directives of vice-chancellor M Junaid Bushiri.The discussions focused on incorporating the National Education Policy provisions, strengthening industry-academia collaboration and promoting holistic student development. Experts from industry, academia, legal practice and technology participated in the sessions.The workshops explored the inclusion of areas such as artificial intelligence, legal technology, financial technology, cyber law, corporate governance, environmental, social and governance (ESG) practices, entrepreneurship, cybersecurity, talent management and technology-driven services. The discussions also focused on developing industry-ready skills and updating law programmes, including BBA LLB, BCom LLB and LLM.Cusat had in Sept decided to introduce the industry-flexible curriculum system to enable universities to respond more quickly to changes in industry, science and technology.Under the proposed model, 80% of the curriculum will comprise core subjects approved by the board of studies, while 20% will consist of components that can be revised periodically. This flexible portion is intended to accommodate emerging technologies, research findings, interdisciplinary learning, industry practices and contemporary developments without requiring a complete overhaul of the curriculum.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news.
